newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION-SAFRICA MAY MISS BUDGET TARGET-BY E.OSBORN.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-SAFRICA MAY MISS BUDGET TARGET-BY E.OSBORN.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

The budget for 1997/98, being as much a political statement as a fiscal plan, aimed to achieve a four percent deficit with Procrustean exactness, involving a 6.1 percent increase in expenditure and a 11.1 percent rise in revenue.
The budget was in line with the fiscal objectives of the Growth, Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy policy of government.

Although too early to be categorical about the eventual outcome, the first quarter's results are suggesting that the fiscal flows are not running according to the budgetary plan; they may also be beginning to expose the lack of reality in the budget with regard to possible restraints on expenditure and the excessive optimism on the revenue side.
Additionally, however, the first quarter's results are interesting in themselves from the point of the financing of the deficit and the impact on national financial flows.

Adjusted first quarter revenue has grown by 7.1 percent, as against the budgeted expected growth for the year of 11.1 percent, and adjusted expenditure by 11.3 percent, as against the planned 6.1 percent for the year -- almost as if there has been an interchange of revenue and expenditure.

However, from past experience there is clearly a tardiness in revenue collection but a smart take-off in expenditure in the first quarter, which makes it difficult to project the outcome for the full year.

The deficit of adjusted current revenue and expenditure flows into and out of the exchequer for the quarter was 12.5 billion, which is slightly more than half the budget deficit for the full year of 24.8 billion rand, already. There should be a distinct slowing down of the deficit generation in the second and third quarters, however, which will improve matters. But at this stage it does appear that the budget's noble deficit goals are not going to be achieved.
A deficit of closer to five percent of gross domestic product is on the cards.

But this is by-the-bye at this stage. The point of concern, however, is the evidence of expenditure pressure in the first quarter figures. Although total expenditure has grown by 11.3 percent, non-interest expenditure has grown by 12.9 percent, and the non-interest expenditure in the first quarter represents 28.5 percent of the budgeted figures.

In particular, the disbursements to the provinces have been between 28 percent and 30 percent of budget. Despite constitutional restraints and fine words the provinces are just going to run into deficits that will have to be made good in the adjustment budget next February.

Financing of the deficit has presented no problems at all and, indeed, has been more than sufficient, resulting in a 3.3 billion rand accumulation of balances at the Reserve Bank and the Tax and Loan Accounts with the private sector banks. In addition the proceeds of the Yankee loan, amounting to 2.2 billion rand, raised in June were retained abroad and should only be sold to the Reserve Bank and added to domestic balances in July.

In all, 18 billion rand net financing income accrued to the Exchequer. Apart from surrenders, the main items included capital receipts of 1.25 billion rand from the Strategic Oil Fund, 1.2 billion rand from the sale of Telkom representing monies from abroad, 8.6 billion rand net issues of domestic stock, 3.5 billion rand from foreign loans and 3.1 billion rand from short-term Treasury bills.

As compared with the budgetary financing programme, the foreign borrowing plans have already been achieved, and the domestic stock issues are somewhat ahead of schedule at 32 percent of the budgetary plan. The Telkom proceeds are nearly 650 million rand more than expected at the time of the Budget.

The accumulation of short-term debt has also apparently been hasty at three billion rand, as compared with two billion rand expected for the whole year but, no doubt, there could be a reduction phase later in the year should management of the financial markets require it.

That the substantial 12.5 billion rand deficit in the quarter did not provide a fiscal fillip to the economy confirms that expenditure patterns are not disturbed by temporary fluctuations in net incomes.
Of greater significance, though, the deficit was more than offset by capital flows into the government coffers, which meant an effective drain of money supply from the private sector to government.

This contributed to the relative stabilisation of money supply during the period, notwithstanding a continuing generation of money through credit creation and an overall surplus on combined balance of payments accounts.

Moreover, the apparently unnecessary increase in short-term borrowings was part of a mopping up operation in the money market which was becoming awash with liquidity through the capital account of the balance of payments.
The Reserve Bank would have felt it necessary to sustain a high level of money market shortage and hence money market rates at a time when it would be premature to release the brakes on Bank rate.
The time was approaching to take the step into the unknown with regard to the relaxation of exchange controls with the 200,000 foreign investment allowance.

A further motivation for the build-up in government balances despite the large deficit would be to prepare for the massive interest payments of nearly nine billion rand that have to be made in August.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
